paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Peters took place in Reno, Nevada, in September 1903, after Peters, a Black man, was arrested on a charge of assaulting a white woman, Mrs. John Dotta. Fearing a lynching, police moved him to the county jail, and a night of rumors and street-corner gatherings ended without an attack. The story reached other Nevada papers through the Reno Journal, and one ran it under the headline "Should Have Lynched Him."

According to the Reno Journal, Peters, "commonly called 'Harry'," had been drinking when he entered the lodging house John Dotta kept over the Reno Wholesale Liquor Store. The Journal said he found Mrs. Dotta making a bed, locked the door and seized her, and that her screams sent a lodger to her husband's Opera House saloon. By the time Dotta returned with Officer Tatum, Peters had fled; Tatum later arrested him at the south entrance of the Virginia street subway and took him to the city jail. Briefs in Elko and Silver City papers placed the incident on Monday, which matches the Journal's "yesterday."

As word of the charge spread, the officers feared an attempt to lynch Peters, and Officers Berry and Tatum moved him to the county jail "for safe-keeping." A later Journal report called the following night "one of vague alarms," with gatherings on street corners and whispered talk of advancing on the jail. In its words, an attack "seemed at one time" certain, "but wiser counsel prevailed."

The Lyon County Times reported that no further trouble was feared by the officers. The Journal also repeated the officers' accusation that Peters was a "rounder" who lived off the earnings "of a woman of his own color," a claim reported only from the police. No report of an indictment, trial or sentence appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage came from white Nevada papers and traced back to the Reno Journal, whose original issues were not among the papers found. The Daily Silver State of Winnemucca reprinted both Journal reports on September 9 under the headlines "Should Have Lynched Him" and "Negro Fiend in Reno Assaults a White Woman," while the Gardnerville Record reprinted the first report on September 11 as "Negro Assaults a White Woman." The Journal text called Peters a "brute" and a "black fiend" and stated the assault as fact, and it remarked that without the transfer he "might be hanging to the Virginia street bridge today."

The Elko Weekly Independent and the Lyon County Times reduced the story to single sentences in their news columns, each noting the talk of lynching without comment. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Peters
bases: Officers moved Peters to the county jail because they feared a lynching, and crowds gathered overnight with talk of advancing on the jail, but no attack was made (A1, A3, A4).

No one was killed: the papers report only rumors, street-corner gatherings and talk of storming the jail, after which 'wiser counsel prevailed' (A1, A4). The threat was tied to an accusation of assault on a white woman (A1), but the episode remained a threatened lynching.
All four items trace to the Reno Journal: A1 and A2 reprint it by name, and the briefs in A3 and A4 condense the same facts, so no independent report was found.

accounts.gist: Peters, drinking, seized Mrs. Dotta in a locked room, fled, and was arrested; fearing a lynching, officers moved him to the county jail, and a night of rumors and gatherings ended without an attack.

accounts.gist: Officers accused Peters of being a 'rounder' who lived off the earnings of a Black woman; this comes only from the officers via the Journal.

framing.detail: The Daily Silver State headlined the Journal reprint 'Should Have Lynched Him' and 'Negro Fiend in Reno Assaults a White Woman'.
Elko and Silver City papers ran one-sentence items stating the assault as fact and noting the lynching talk without comment.

conflicts.note: Not a real conflict: the reprint's 'yesterday' refers to the original Journal issue, which was likely September 8, so all versions fit Monday, September 7.

quotes: If he hadn't been taken from the city prison to the more inviunerable structure he might be hanging to the Virginia street bridge today.
